questions.figureAlt: A lever on a fulcrum. A 100-pound weight sits 3 feet to the left of the fulcrum. An unknown downward force pushes 6 feet to the right of the fulcrum.
questions.question: How much force is needed at the right end to balance the lever?
questions.explanation:
A lever balances when weight × distance is the same on both sides.
100 lb × 3 ft = 300.
Force × 6 ft = 300, so force = 50 lb.
The longer arm needs less force.

questions.figureAlt: A lever on a fulcrum. A 60-pound weight sits 4 feet to the left of the fulcrum. A 40-pound weight sits an unknown distance to the right.
questions.question: How far from the fulcrum must the 40-pound weight sit to balance the lever?
questions.explanation:
Balance: weight × distance must match on both sides.
60 × 4 = 240.
40 × distance = 240, so distance = 6 ft.
The lighter weight has to sit farther out.

questions.question: A lever has an effort arm 8 feet long and a load arm 2 feet long. What is its mechanical advantage?
questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage = effort arm ÷ load arm = 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Each pound of effort lifts 4 pounds.

questions.question: Which of these is a second-class lever, with the load between the fulcrum and the effort?
questions.explanation: In a wheelbarrow, the wheel is the fulcrum, the load is in the middle and you lift at the handles. A seesaw is first-class (fulcrum in the middle). Tweezers and fishing rods are third-class (effort in the middle).

questions.question: On a lever, moving the fulcrum closer to the load makes the load:
choices: No easier or harder to lift
questions.explanation: Moving the fulcrum toward the load makes the effort arm longer and the load arm shorter, so less force is needed. The trade-off: you push through a longer distance.

questions.question: In a first-class lever, where is the fulcrum?
choices: Between the effort and the load
At one end, with the load in the middle
At one end, with the effort in the middle
questions.explanation: First class: fulcrum in the middle (seesaw, crowbar). Second class: load in the middle (wheelbarrow). Third class: effort in the middle (broom, tweezers).

questions.question: In a third-class lever, such as a broom, the effort is between the fulcrum and the load. Compared with the effort, the load:
choices: Moves farther and faster, but more force is needed
Moves a shorter distance, and less force is needed
Moves the same distance with the same force
questions.explanation: A third-class lever always needs more force than the load, but it moves the load farther and faster. That's why a broom or bat swings its end so quickly.

questions.figureAlt: A single pulley attached to the ceiling. A rope runs over it from a 100-pound weight to a person pulling down on the other end.
questions.question: Ignoring friction, how much force is needed to lift the 100-pound weight?
questions.explanation: A single fixed pulley doesn't reduce the force. It only changes its direction, so you can pull down to lift up. Mechanical advantage = 1.

questions.figureAlt: A rope tied to the ceiling runs down under a pulley that holds a 100-pound weight, then back up to a person pulling up.
questions.question: Ignoring friction and the pulley's weight, how much force is needed to lift the 100-pound weight?
questions.explanation: Two rope segments hold up the movable pulley, so each carries half the load: 100 ÷ 2 = 50 lb. The trade-off: you pull 2 feet of rope for every foot the weight rises.

questions.figureAlt: A block and tackle: an upper pulley block attached to the ceiling and a lower block holding a 200-pound weight, with four rope segments between the blocks and a free end pulled down.
questions.question: Ignoring friction, how much force is needed to lift the 200-pound weight?
questions.explanation: Count the rope segments holding up the lower block: 4. Force = 200 ÷ 4 = 50 lb. The free end you pull doesn't count, because it doesn't hold up the load.

questions.question: A pulley system has a mechanical advantage of 2. To raise a load 3 feet, how much rope must you pull?
questions.explanation: Machines trade force for distance. With a mechanical advantage of 2, you use half the force but pull twice as far: 3 × 2 = 6 feet.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a single fixed pulley?
choices: It changes the direction of the force
It cuts the force needed in half
questions.explanation: A single fixed pulley lets you pull down to lift something up, which is easier and safer, but it doesn't reduce the force.

questions.question: In a block and tackle, three rope segments hold up the load. Ignoring friction, how much force lifts 300 pounds?
questions.explanation: Force = load ÷ supporting segments = 300 ÷ 3 = 100 lb.

questions.figureAlt: Two meshed gears, A and B. Gear A turns clockwise.
questions.question: Gear A turns clockwise. Which way does gear B turn?
questions.explanation: Two meshed gears always turn in opposite directions.

questions.figureAlt: Three gears in a row, A, B and C, each meshed with the next. Gear A turns clockwise.
questions.question: Gear A turns clockwise. Which way does gear C turn?
questions.explanation: Each meshed gear reverses direction: A clockwise, B counterclockwise, C clockwise. In a row of gears, every other gear turns the same way.

questions.figureAlt: Two meshed gears: gear A has 10 teeth and gear B has 30 teeth.
questions.question: Gear A turns 3 full times. How many times does gear B turn?
questions.explanation: A turning 3 times moves 3 × 10 = 30 teeth past the contact point. B has 30 teeth, so it turns 30 ÷ 30 = 1 time.

questions.figureAlt: Two meshed gears: gear A has 10 teeth and gear B has 30 teeth.
questions.question: Which gear turns faster?
choices: Both turn at the same speed
It depends on which way they turn
questions.explanation: The smaller gear must turn more times to keep up with the larger one. Here A turns 3 times for every 1 turn of B.

questions.figureAlt: Two pulleys joined by a belt that runs straight from one to the other. The driver pulley on the left turns clockwise.
questions.question: The driver pulley turns clockwise. Which way does the other pulley turn?
questions.explanation: With a straight (open) belt, both pulleys turn the same direction.

questions.figureAlt: Two pulleys joined by a belt that crosses over itself in the middle. The driver pulley on the left turns clockwise.
questions.question: The driver pulley turns clockwise. Which way does the other pulley turn?
questions.explanation: A crossed belt reverses direction, so the second pulley turns counterclockwise.

questions.question: When a small gear drives a large gear, the large gear turns:
choices: Slower, but with more turning force
Faster, but with less turning force
At the same speed and force
questions.explanation: Gearing trades speed for turning force (torque). A small gear driving a large one gives more torque and less speed, like low gear on a bike.

questions.question: A 12-tooth gear turning at 90 revolutions per minute drives a 36-tooth gear. How fast does the 36-tooth gear turn?
questions.explanation:
Speed changes in the opposite ratio to the teeth: 36 ÷ 12 = 3, so the larger gear turns 3 times slower.
90 ÷ 3 = 30 rpm.

questions.figureAlt: A 200-pound box on a ramp 12 feet long that rises 3 feet.
questions.question: Ignoring friction, how much force is needed to push the box up the ramp?
questions.explanation:
Mechanical advantage of a ramp = length ÷ height = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
Force = 200 ÷ 4 = 50 lb.

questions.question: Compared with a short, steep ramp to the same height, a longer ramp needs:
choices: Less force, over a longer distance
More force, over a shorter distance
questions.explanation: A longer ramp is less steep, so it takes less force, but you push the load farther. The work done is about the same.

questions.question: A screw is really a type of:
choices: Inclined plane wrapped around a post
questions.explanation: A screw's thread is a ramp wound around a shaft. Each turn pushes the screw forward a small distance with great force.

questions.question: Compared with a coarse-thread screw of the same size, a fine-thread screw:
choices: Takes more turns to go in the same distance
Takes fewer turns to go in the same distance
questions.explanation: Fine threads are closer together, so each turn moves the screw a shorter distance. It takes more turns but less force per turn, and it holds tightly.

questions.question: An axe head is an example of which simple machine?
questions.explanation: A wedge turns a downward force into a force that pushes material apart. Axes, knives and doorstops are wedges.

questions.question: A steering wheel with a 10-inch radius turns a shaft with a 1-inch radius. What is the mechanical advantage?
questions.explanation: Wheel and axle: mechanical advantage = wheel radius ÷ axle radius = 10 ÷ 1 = 10.

questions.question: Which of these is a wheel and axle?
questions.explanation: Turning the large knob turns the small shaft inside the door with more force. Screwdrivers and steering wheels work the same way.

questions.question: How much work is done pushing a cart with a force of 50 pounds for 20 feet?
questions.explanation: Work = force × distance = 50 × 20 = 1,000 foot-pounds.

questions.question: In which case is no work done on the box?
choices: Pushing a box across the floor
Lifting a box onto a shelf
Carrying a box up the stairs
questions.explanation: In physics, work means force times distance moved. Holding a box still is tiring, but the box doesn't move, so no work is done on it.

questions.question: What reduces friction between moving metal parts?
questions.explanation: Lubricants put a thin slippery layer between surfaces. Ball bearings also cut friction by rolling instead of sliding.

questions.question: Why is a tall, narrow load more likely to tip over than a short, wide one?
choices: Its center of gravity is higher and its base is narrower
questions.explanation: An object tips when its center of gravity moves past the edge of its base. A high center of gravity over a narrow base gets there sooner. Keep loads low and wide.

questions.question: A spring stretches 2 inches under a 10-pound weight. How far does it stretch under a 30-pound weight?
questions.explanation: Within its limit, a spring stretches in proportion to the force. Three times the weight gives three times the stretch: 2 × 3 = 6 inches.

questions.question: Machine A does the same work as machine B in half the time. Machine A has:
questions.explanation: Power = work ÷ time. The same work in half the time means twice the power.

questions.question: A car takes a sharp curve to the left. Loose items on the dashboard slide:
choices: To the right, toward the outside of the curve
To the left, toward the inside of the curve
questions.explanation: Inertia keeps the items moving in a straight line while the car turns under them, so they slide toward the outside of the curve.

questions.question: On a spinning wheel, which point moves fastest?
choices: A point on the outer rim
A point halfway to the rim
A point next to the hub
Every point moves at the same speed
questions.explanation: Every point makes one turn in the same time, but a point on the rim travels the largest circle, so it moves fastest.

questions.question: Why can no real machine be 100% efficient?
choices: Some energy is always lost to friction and heat
questions.explanation: Friction turns some input energy into heat, so the useful output is always less than the input.

questions.figureAlt: A hydraulic press: a small piston with an area of 2 square inches pushed down with 10 pounds, connected by fluid to a large piston with an area of 20 square inches.
questions.question: How much upward force does the large piston produce?
questions.explanation:
Pressure is the same throughout the fluid: 10 lb ÷ 2 sq in = 5 pounds per square inch.
Large piston: 5 × 20 = 100 lb.
The large piston moves a shorter distance, so energy is still conserved.

questions.question: A 120-pound force presses on an area of 4 square inches. What is the pressure?
questions.explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 psi.

questions.figureAlt: A tall water tank with three holes in its side: A near the top, B in the middle and C near the bottom.
questions.question: At which hole is the water pressure greatest?
choices: The pressure is the same at all three
questions.explanation: Water pressure increases with depth, because there's more water above pushing down. Hole C is deepest.

questions.question: Why are dams built thicker at the bottom than at the top?
choices: Water is warmer at the bottom
Concrete is cheaper at the bottom
questions.explanation: The deeper the water, the more pressure it puts on the dam, so the bottom must be strongest.

questions.question: Hydraulic brakes and lifts work because liquids:
questions.explanation: A liquid barely compresses, so a push at one end is passed through it to the other end. That's Pascal's principle.

questions.question: Why does a steel ship float?
choices: It pushes aside water weighing as much as the ship
questions.explanation: A floating object displaces water equal to its own weight. A ship's hollow hull pushes aside enough water to balance its weight (Archimedes' principle).

questions.question: Gas in a sealed, rigid container is heated. What happens to its pressure?
questions.explanation: Heat makes gas molecules move faster and hit the container walls harder and more often, so pressure rises. That's why aerosol cans warn against heat.
